section.title: The Woman on the Beast
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 17 pauses the sequence of judgment to unpack, through an angel-guided vision and explicit interpretation, exactly who Babylon the great is: an idolatrous, blood-guilty empire pictured as a prostitute riding a monstrous beast. It is bounded by the angel's invitation in 17:1 to see the prostitute's punishment and the identification of the woman as the great city in 17:18, forming a self-contained interpretive unit between the bowls and Babylon's fall.
section.thesis: Babylon the great, an alluring alliance of idolatrous empire, wealth, and false religion, rides on the very beast that will one day turn and devour her, while the Lamb, though warred against by the kings of the earth, triumphs as Lord of lords and King of kings.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the angel's invitation to see the prostitute's judgment; the vision of the woman enthroned on the scarlet beast; the angel's interpretation of the beast, its heads, and its kings; the ten horns' war against the Lamb and His certain triumph; and the meaning of the waters and the woman as the great city that rules the kings of the earth.

units.label: The invitation to see the prostitute's judgment

verses.text: Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the punishment of the great {{porne|prostitute}}, who sits on many waters.
The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and those who dwell on the earth were intoxicated with the wine of her immorality.”

units.label: The vision: the woman on the scarlet beast
units.note: dazzling, drunk with the blood of the saints

verses.text: And the angel carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, where I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet {{therion|beast}} that was covered with blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns.
The woman was dressed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls. She held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
And on her forehead a {{mysterion|mysterious}} name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.
I could see that the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus. And I was utterly amazed at the sight of her.

units.label: The angel explains the beast, its heads, and its kings
units.note: a mind with wisdom is required

verses.text: “Why are you so amazed?” said the angel. “I will tell you the {{mysterion|mystery}} of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and ten horns.

The beast that you saw, it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the {{abyssos|Abyss}} and go to its destruction. And those who dwell on the earth whose names were not written in the Book of Life from the foundation of the world will marvel when they see the beast that was, and is not, and yet will be.
This calls for a mind with wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits.
There are also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come; but when he does come, he must remain for only a little while.
The beast that was, and now is not, is an eighth king, who belongs to the other seven and is going into destruction.

units.label: The ten horns' war and the Lamb's triumph
units.note: Lord of lords and King of kings

verses.text: The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive one hour of authority as kings, along with the beast.
These kings have one purpose: to yield their power and authority to the beast.

They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is {{kyrios|Lord}} of lords and King of kings; and He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.”

units.label: The waters, the beast's hatred, and the meaning of the woman
units.note: the great city that rules the kings of the earth

verses.text: Then the angel said to me, “The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues.
And the ten horns and the beast that you saw will hate the prostitute. They will leave her desolate and naked, and will eat her flesh and burn her with fire.
For God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.
And the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.”

porne.gloss: A prostitute or harlot. The word pictures a woman who sells herself, deliberately paired throughout the chapter with porneia, sexual immorality, itself a stock Old Testament metaphor for idolatry and covenant unfaithfulness, Hosea, Ezekiel 16, Jeremiah 3. Babylon the great is not literal prostitution but an empire whose idolatrous, seductive power draws the nations away from the true God.

therion.gloss: A wild beast, a monster. The word Revelation uses throughout for the persecuting political power introduced in chapter 13. Here the beast carries the woman, showing that the world's idolatrous religious and economic system rides upon, and is ultimately used and discarded by, brute political power.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a hidden truth now disclosed. In the New Testament a mysterion is not something obscure forever but a secret God chooses to unveil; here the angel promises to explain the mystery of the woman and the beast, and does so plainly in the verses that follow, showing that apocalyptic symbols are meant to be understood, not left as riddles.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master, owner. Used throughout the Greek Old Testament to render the divine name, the title here crowns Jesus as Lord of lords, sovereign over every earthly king who wars against Him; His triumph is not future speculation but the certain outcome already declared.

abyssos.gloss: The abyss, the bottomless pit. Revelation's name for the prison of demonic powers, from which the beast emerges and to which it returns for final destruction; its appearance here anchors the beast's power as derivative and temporary, in contrast to the everlasting kingdom of Christ.

basic.context: An angel takes John in a vision to see a woman, a prostitute called Babylon, riding on a monstrous, many-headed beast. She is dressed in splendor and drunk with the blood of God's people, and the angel explains that the beast and its heads and horns stand for a succession of kings and kingdoms that will make war on the Lamb, and lose. In the end the very beast that carries the woman turns on her, and the vision explains that she is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.
basic.hermeneutics: The identity of Babylon here is one of the most debated pictures in Revelation, whether it refers mainly to the Rome of John's own day, some future world system, or the recurring pattern of idolatrous civilization in every age, allied with worldly power. The debate is worth naming honestly rather than settling too quickly, but the chapter's central claims are not in doubt: this seductive alliance of empire and idolatry will be judged, will be destroyed by its own ally, and the Lamb will triumph regardless of how any reader identifies the details.
basic.originalLanguages: Babylon is a porne, a prostitute, the Old Testament's regular picture for idolatry dressed up as allure. She rides a therion, a beast, the same word for the persecuting power of chapter 13. The angel promises to unveil the mysterion, the mystery, showing that the vision's symbols are meant to be understood, not left as an unsolvable riddle. And at the chapter's center, Jesus is named kyrios of lords, Lord of lords, guaranteeing His victory over every power that wars against Him.
basic.typology: Babylon's portrait as a bejeweled, seductive prostitute drunk on the blood of the saints draws directly on Old Testament pictures of idolatrous nations and unfaithful cities, now brought to their final form and final judgment.
basic.christ: In the middle of this dark vision stands one certain fact: the Lamb triumphs. Every king who wars against Him loses, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings, and His called, chosen, and faithful people share in that victory with Him.
basic.god: God's sovereignty extends even over evil's self-destruction: it is God who puts it into the hearts of the beast and the ten horns to turn on the prostitute and destroy her, showing that even the alliance of evil powers unknowingly serves God's determined purpose.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 51 and Isaiah 47 picture Babylon as a queen and sorceress judged by God. Ezekiel 16 and Hosea use the same image for unfaithful Israel. And Revelation 19 shows the Lamb's promised triumph finally realized as He returns as King of kings and Lord of lords.
basic.oneStory: From Israel's prophets to Revelation's final vision, Scripture pictures idolatry as adultery and empire as prostitution, seductive, wealthy, and ultimately self-destructive. But running through every page is the promise that the Lamb, however fiercely warred against, triumphs, and all who are called, chosen, and faithful triumph with Him.

context.literary:
Chapter 17 is the one place in Revelation where a vision is followed at once by an angel's explanation. John is invited to see, he sees, he is amazed, and the angel then asks why he is amazed and interprets the picture in verses 7 to 18. That structure alone tells us the symbols are meant to be understood. The chapter divides cleanly in two: verses 1 to 6 are what John sees, verses 7 to 18 are what the angel says. Within the explanation there are three turns. The angel explains the beast, its heads and its kings, verses 8 to 11. He explains the horns and their war against the Lamb, verses 12 to 14. He explains the waters and the woman, verses 15 to 18. The movement ends where the book began, with a statement about who rules.

The chapter is also built as a deliberate counterpart to chapter 21. In 17:1 'one of the seven angels with the seven bowls' invites John with the words 'Come, I will show you,' carries him away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and shows him a woman. In 21:9 and 21:10 the same sort of angel with the same invitation carries him in the Spirit to a great and high mountain and shows him the bride, the wife of the Lamb. The two women, the two cities and the two places of seeing are set against each other. The chapter also contains a mock of the divine name, since the beast 'was, and is not, and is about to come up,' a distorted echo of the God 'who is and who was and who is to come.'
context.historical:
The first readers would have recognised the picture without a key. Rome was the city on seven hills, and the poets of the empire praised it by that very feature. Rome was also the city that ruled 'over the kings of the earth,' as verse 18 says, since client kings held their thrones by its favour. The purple and scarlet, gold, jewels and pearls were the dress of wealth and power, and the goddess Roma was worshiped in the cities of Asia. The list of seven kings in verses 9 to 11 invites a count of emperors, though the beginning point of the count has been argued and no agreement exists. Whatever the count, the picture of a city that is both prostitute and patron fitted the Roman order: it gave peace and prosperity to those who joined its worship and its trade, and it was drunk with the blood of those who would not.

Yet John does not simply say 'Rome.' The woman sits on 'many waters,' and the angel says they are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues. Babylon in the Old Testament was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and carried the people into exile, and it stood for pride and idolatry. Using the old name allowed John to name a power by its character and not only its address, and to say that the next empire, and the one after, would be the same Babylon again. The wilderness setting is also telling. In the Bible the wilderness is the place of testing and of encounter, and John sees the woman there without any of the splendour of her city.
context.canonical:
The portrait of the prostitute assembles the prophets' pictures of cities that gave their love to other gods. Nineveh is a harlot who betrays nations by her prostitution, Nahum 3:4. Tyre is pictured as a prostitute selling herself to the kingdoms of the earth, Isaiah 23:15 to 17. Jerusalem herself is the faithless wife of Ezekiel 16 and 23 and of Hosea. Babylon is addressed as one who 'dwells by many waters' in Jeremiah 51:13 and is a gold cup in the Lord's hand 'making the whole earth drunk' in Jeremiah 51:7. Revelation draws on all of these. The seven heads and ten horns come from the dragon of 12:3 and the beast of 13:1, and in turn from Daniel 7, where the ten horns are ten kings, Daniel 7:24.

The New Testament frames the chapter's outcome. The title 'Lord of lords and King of kings' in verse 14 comes from Deuteronomy 10:17 and from Daniel 2:47, and it returns in 19:16 and in 1 Timothy 6:15. The book of Life in verse 8 returns in 20:12 and 21:27. The 'wine of her immorality' becomes the cup of God's wrath in 14:8 and 16:19. And the next chapter, Revelation 18, will quote Isaiah and Jeremiah heavily in announcing her end. The woman's counterpart, the bride in 19:7 and 21:2, makes the choice between two cities and two loves the book's final interpretive frame.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John's first aim is to tell the churches that the empire's glamour is a lie. The woman is dressed in purple, scarlet, gold and pearls, and carries a golden cup. But the cup is full of abominations, her name is a 'mystery,' and she is drunk with the blood of the saints. The angel strips the splendour away: this is not the goddess of a thriving city but an adulteress, and her allies will hate her in the end. For Christians who felt the pull of belonging to such a world, or who suffered for refusing it, the chapter changes what they are looking at.

His second aim is to give them courage. The beast and the kings have power, but only 'one hour,' and only until God's words are fulfilled. They will make war on the Lamb, and the outcome is stated in advance. Their numbers do not matter, since the Lamb is Lord of lords and King of kings. The people with Him are called, chosen and faithful, and they are not asked to win a battle but to be found with Him.

His third aim is to call for wisdom. 'This calls for a mind with wisdom,' he says in verse 9, and the saints are expected to think through what they are told, to resist being amazed as John was, and to see where power is leading. The hearers who did not marvel were those whose names were written in the Book of Life.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a vision and explains it. It does not issue a program. The only commands are implicit: do not be amazed by the beast, which the text contrasts with the amazement of those who dwell on the earth, and use wisdom. The description of the prostitute as drunk with the blood of the saints is a report, and the description of the kings burning her with fire is a report of what God will bring about through them, not an instruction for anyone to do the same.

Readers must also be careful not to take the details as a licence to name a modern enemy. The woman is called 'the great city that rules over the kings of the earth,' and many churches have used that phrase against their opponents. History shows how often this has been done, and how often it has been wrong. The text points to a pattern of idolatrous power joined with wealth and religion, and the pattern is recognisable in every age. What the passage prescribes by implication is the hard work of examining one's own life for the seductions it describes: the wine of her immorality, the comfort that comes from compromise, and the awe of a power that seems unbeatable. It also teaches Christians not to be proud of their own side, because the call in 18:4 is for God's people to come out of her.

debates.question: Who is the woman, Babylon the great?

views.label: Rome, the city of seven hills
views.case: The seven mountains of verse 9 point to Rome, and verse 18 says the woman is the city that rules the kings of the earth, which was Rome's position in John's day. Early Christian writers commonly read it this way. The kings, the trade and the persecution fit the empire the churches knew.

views.label: A future world system or religious-political power
views.case: Because the text speaks of an alliance that rises at the end, joined with the beast and ten kings, some expect a future revived empire or a global religious and commercial order. They point out that the vision covers more than any first-century city, since she sits on many waters, which are all nations.

views.label: The recurring pattern of godless civilisation in every age
views.case: Others hold that Babylon is a type that appears in every empire that combines political power, wealth and idolatry. Rome was one embodiment, and others have followed. On this view 'Babylon' is a symbol that does not wait for one city.

debates.bearing: All three readings hold that the woman stands for a seductive, blood-guilty alliance of power, wealth and false worship, and that God will bring it down. The shared conclusion is the one the text itself underlines: do not be amazed by her, and do not be found in her.

debates.question: How are the seven kings of verses 9 to 11 to be counted?

views.label: A count of Roman emperors
views.case: Five have fallen, one is, and one has not yet come. Counting emperors from Augustus or from Julius Caesar, an interpreter finds the 'one is' in or near John's day. The eighth who 'belongs to the other seven' is then a figure of renewed persecution, often tied to Nero's expected return.

views.label: A symbolic number for a full sweep of world powers
views.case: Seven is the number of completeness in Revelation, and the five, the one and the other suggest successive world empires such as Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia and Greece, with Rome the sixth. The seventh and the eighth are future. The count is a way of placing the church in the long line of empires.

views.label: A future set of rulers, not a historical list
views.case: A further view treats the whole sequence as yet to come, with no relation to past emperors, because the seven heads represent a final series of kings in the end times, with the beast as an eighth who belongs to them.

debates.bearing: None of these counts can be shown to be the only correct one, and the angel himself says it calls for wisdom. What is clear is the pattern: the powers rise and fall, the last of them is destroyed, and none of them lasts past God's words.

study.originalLanguages:
John makes his points through a handful of verbs that English tends to flatten. The kings of the earth 'were immoral with her,' which is the verb porneuo, and the earth's inhabitants are 'intoxicated' with her wine, methyo, the verb for being drunk. The woman herself, in verse 6, is 'drunk' with the blood of the saints, the same verb. The reversal is intentional: the nations are drunk on her wine, and she is drunk on their martyrs. The vocabulary of drunkenness carries a sense of loss of judgment, and it fits a city that does not see where it is going.

The verb 'amazed' is another small key. John says in verse 6 that he was 'utterly amazed,' and the Greek is ethaumasa with a noun of the same root, thauma mega, a great wonder. The angel's question in verse 7 uses the same verb. In verse 8 those whose names are not in the Book of Life 'will marvel' at the beast, thaumasontai, using it again. John is caught in the very response that the earth's inhabitants will show, and the angel's question corrects him. Wonder is the right response to God, and the beast calls it out falsely.

Verse 8 also parodies the divine name. The beast 'was, and now is no more, but is about to come up,' and 'was, and is not, and yet will be.' The phrasing borrows the shape of the title for God in 1:4 and 1:8, 'who is and who was and who is to come,' but the beast's middle term is 'is not.' It is a counterfeit of resurrection and of eternal being.

In verses 13 and 17 the word gnome, mind or purpose, appears. The kings have 'one purpose,' mian gnomen, to give their power to the beast. In verse 17 God 'has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose,' ten gnomen autou, and to act with 'one purpose' again. The same word is used of both their plan and His, and the second swallows the first. The phrase 'until the words of God are fulfilled' uses a verb of completion, telesthesontai, related to the verb used of the plagues being 'completed' in 15:1 and 15:8.

typology.type: Babylon as the city of pride and exile
typology.fulfillment: The historical Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and exiled its people, and the prophets answered with oracles of its fall, Isaiah 47 and Jeremiah 50 and 51. Isaiah called her one who said, 'I will be queen forever,' Isaiah 47:7. John takes the name and makes it a pattern: the Babylon of Revelation 17 has the same pride and the same sorcery and the same violence. The escalation is that the city now stands for all human systems that exalt themselves and persecute God's people. The type falls short in that ancient Babylon was one place, and the final Babylon is not limited to any single location.

The prophets used marriage to describe God's covenant with His people, and unfaithfulness to Him as adultery or prostitution, Ezekiel 16, Hosea 1 to 3, Jeremiah 3. In Revelation 17 the image is applied to an empire and its religion, and set against the bride of the Lamb in 19:7 to 8 and 21:2. Christ is the faithful bridegroom whom Paul presents a pure virgin to, 2 Corinthians 11:2, while the harlot is the system that leads people away from Him. The correspondence falls short in that the unfaithful wife of the prophets was a people who could return, as Hosea's wife did, while this woman is given a sentence.

The beast's career is a parody of Christ's. It 'was, and is not, and will be,' it has a throne given by the dragon, it receives worship, and it gathers a following with a mark. Against it stands the Lamb, once slain and now alive, and the contrast is the book's constant theme. The ten horns, 'ten kings,' recall Daniel 7:24. The escalation is that Daniel's beasts were kingdoms in succession while Revelation sees them gathered in one last blasphemous system. The type falls short as a copy: the beast can imitate, but cannot create life, and its 'return' ends in destruction.

Jeremiah 51:7 calls Babylon a gold cup in the Lord's hand that made the whole earth drunk, and the Old Testament has a second cup, the cup of the Lord's wrath that the nations must drink, Jeremiah 25:15 to 16. In Revelation 17:4 the woman holds a golden cup full of abominations, and in 16:19 God gives her His cup. Jesus took up the cup of wrath at Gethsemane, Matthew 26:39, and offered a different cup at the table, the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20. The types converge: the cup that the nations drink is turned back on the one who gave it, and the cup of mercy is given by the Lamb.

study.christ:
The centre of this dark chapter is a single sentence in verse 14: 'They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them.' Everything else in the chapter is the setting for it. The vision of the prostitute and the beast is a vision of what the world will turn against Jesus, and the angel's explanation is that the contest has already been decided, since He is Lord of lords and King of kings. Two aspects of the verse repay attention.

First, the title. 'Lord of lords and King of kings' was said of the God of Israel in Deuteronomy 10:17 and Daniel 2:47, and Paul gave it to the one Sovereign in 1 Timothy 6:15. Here the title is the reason given for the Lamb's triumph, 'because He is,' and so Christ is placed where the Old Testament placed God. The contrast with the kings is exact. They have 'one hour' of authority and they hand it to the beast, while He holds a title that nothing can take.

Second, the means of victory. The Lamb is called a lamb even as He conquers. The word picks up the image of the slain Lamb in chapter 5, so the victory is that of the one who was killed and rose. John never says He will win by outfighting the beast. In 19:15 the sword is in His mouth, His word. The war, in other words, is real and its outcome is not in doubt, but it is a contest that He has already won on the cross, Colossians 2:15.

The chapter also shows the people who share in His triumph. He will be 'accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.' That is a threefold description of His people: they are called by the gospel, chosen by God, and faithful through trial. Those who are with the Lamb are not an army of their own. They are with Him, as the 144,000 were on Zion. The mention of 'faithful' does not make faithfulness a condition of being His, but names the evidence that they are.

Finally, Jesus makes a contrast with the woman in His own person. She is the adulteress, He the bridegroom, and the cup in her hand is full of abominations while the cup in His hand at the supper is His blood. The one is adorned in jewels and in blood, the other in the righteous deeds of the saints, 19:8. In a chapter without a single direct word from Christ, He is the answer to every symbol.
study.god:
The most surprising sentence in the chapter about God is verse 17: 'God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.' The kings believe they are acting for their own interest. They decide to hate the prostitute, burn her and give their kingdom to the beast. Yet the text says it is God who has put the decision into their hearts. This is the same sort of sovereignty that is shown elsewhere in Scripture, where Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant it for good, Genesis 50:20, and where the Lord used Assyria as the rod of His anger, Isaiah 10:5 to 7. Evil is not caused by God, and the kings are responsible for what they choose. But they cannot do anything that falls outside the scope of what He has said.

A second truth is God's faithfulness to His word. The chapter ends with a deadline: the kings reign 'until the words of God are fulfilled.' That phrase pulls the whole of prophecy into the verse. What Isaiah said about Babylon, what Daniel said about the beasts, and what Jesus said about the end, are not forgotten promises but are in process. For the believer it is a reason for patience, and for the persecutor a reason for dread.

A third truth is that God knows His people by name. The Book of Life was written 'from the foundation of the world,' verse 8, which means that those who are not amazed by the beast are those whom God had in view before the beast existed. The people who marvel are the people who do not have their names there. This is God's security for believers: it is not their steadiness but His record that holds. At the same time, the text keeps human accountability, for those who dwell on the earth 'marvel' by their own choice.

For worship, the chapter calls for a sort of sober trust. God is the King who is above the kings, who allows evil powers to proceed to their own end, and who remains holy, just and faithful. It asks believers to praise Him not only for what He does for them but for the fact that no empire, however it glitters, can outlast His words.

crossReferences.note: Babylon is a gold cup in the Lord's hand, making the whole earth drunk, and the nations drank her wine. Revelation 17:2 and 17:4 take up both the cup and the wine. The point is that her power to intoxicate was permitted by God and is now to be judged.

The prophet speaks to Babylon as one who dwells by many waters, rich in treasures, whose end has come. John's 'sits on many waters' in verse 1 uses the same description, and the angel's interpretation in verse 15 turns the waters into peoples.

The virgin daughter of Babylon is brought down from her throne, and she says in her heart, 'I will be queen forever.' The pride, the sorceries and the sudden loss of the earlier Babylon are the pattern for the woman of chapter 17.

Nineveh is the seductive mistress of sorcery who betrays nations by her prostitution. It shows that the prophets used the image of the prostitute for an empire's political and commercial seductions before Revelation did.

Jerusalem, the beloved bride, trusts in her beauty and plays the prostitute with every passer by. The chapter shows how the Old Testament used the image for covenant unfaithfulness, and why Revelation can speak of a religious as well as a political betrayal.

The ten horns are ten kings who rise from the fourth kingdom, and another king subdues three. Revelation 17:12 takes the ten horns as ten kings with a short authority, so that the angel's interpretation continues Daniel's rather than starting afresh.

The beast from the sea with seven heads, ten horns and blasphemous names, and the worship it receives. Chapter 17 identifies the same beast and shows its relation to the woman who rides it, which is why her fate and its are bound together.
The Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords. The source of the title in Revelation 17:14, which shows that the Lamb is given a name that Israel's Scriptures reserved for the one God.

The angel with the seven bowls carries John away in the Spirit to see the bride, the wife of the Lamb. The pairing with 17:1 to 3 makes the two women and the two cities a deliberate contrast, one a harlot in a wilderness and the other a bride on a high mountain.

The name written on the Rider's robe and thigh is King of kings and Lord of lords. The promise of 17:14 is carried out: the Lamb who was warred against appears as the conquering King, and the kings and their armies are overthrown.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis 3 onwards the Bible has told a story of two ways of living. In Genesis 4 Cain builds a city, and in Genesis 11 Babel's people say, 'let us make a name for ourselves.' That impulse, to build a world that secures its own glory without God, reaches its end in Babylon the great. She is the city of Babel, grown up and enriched and armed. In the Bible's other line, Abraham looked for a city whose architect and builder is God, Hebrews 11:10. Chapter 17 shows the first of the two cities at the moment of her fall, and chapter 21 will show the second coming down from heaven.

The woman's picture also gathers up one of the Bible's most persistent images, that sin is a kind of unfaithfulness. God made Israel His own and called Himself her husband. When Israel took other gods, He called it prostitution. Revelation applies the same language to the powers of the world and to any religion that serves them. The cup is the most telling detail. In Eden the choice was a fruit that looked good for food and a delight to the eyes, and the woman's golden cup here is the same offer in its final form: beautiful, rich and deadly. The one who drinks is drunk, and does not see the judgment coming.

The chapter looks back to the promise of Genesis 3:15 as well. The serpent's seed makes war, and the Lamb, the woman's offspring, triumphs. The kings 'will make war against the Lamb,' and the Lamb 'will triumph over them.' The war that began in Eden ends in a single verse. It is not the beast's cunning but the Lamb's title that decides it.

What follows is the fall of Babylon in chapter 18 and the coming of the King in chapter 19, and after the thousand years and the judgment, the new Jerusalem. In that city there is no prostitute and no cup of abominations: nothing impure will ever enter, and only those whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life, 21:27. The Bible's story ends where the faithful are finally with the One they followed, and the false lover who deceived the world has been exposed and gone.

sermon.title: Revelation (Part 20): Revelation 17-18
sermon.why: Carson's sermon covers Revelation 17-18 directly, addressing the vision of the great prostitute drawn from Old Testament prophecy and the contrast between the prostitute and the bride, matching the exact passage and theme of this study.

quiz.q: What does the angel say the woman represents in verse 18?

options.text: The great city that rules over the kings of the earth, an alliance of idolatrous empire and worldly power.
options.note: Revelation 17:18 gives this explicit interpretation.

options.text: A literal individual woman who will appear at the end of history.
options.note: The angel identifies her as a city, a symbol of a system, not a literal individual.

options.text: The bride of the Lamb in disguise.
options.note: She is the great prostitute, the opposite figure to the bride introduced later in Revelation.

options.text: A minor character with no larger significance in the vision.
options.note: She is the central figure of the whole vision, explicitly interpreted by the angel.

quiz.q: What happens to the prostitute at the hands of the beast and its ten horns?

options.text: They turn on her, leaving her desolate and naked, and eat her flesh and burn her with fire.
options.note: Revelation 17:16 describes this reversal.

options.text: They defend and protect her from all future judgment.
options.note: The opposite happens; her own allies destroy her.

options.text: They crown her as their permanent queen.
options.note: They hate her and destroy her rather than honoring her.

options.text: They ignore her and move on to make war on the Lamb alone.
options.note: The text specifically describes their violent turn against her.

quiz.q: Why does the Lamb triumph over the kings who war against Him?

options.text: Because He is Lord of lords and King of kings, accompanied by His called, chosen, and faithful people.
options.note: Revelation 17:14 gives this reason directly.

options.text: Because the kings run out of resources to continue the war.
options.note: The text gives His identity as Lord of lords as the reason, not attrition.

options.text: Because an angel intervenes to disarm them.
options.note: No such angelic disarming is described; the Lamb Himself triumphs.

options.text: The outcome of the war is left genuinely uncertain in the text.
options.note: The text states plainly that the Lamb will triumph over them.

quiz.q: What does the angel promise to explain to John in verse 7?

options.text: The mystery of the woman and the beast that carries her, with its seven heads and ten horns.
options.note: Revelation 17:7 states this explicitly.

options.text: The exact date of the beast's final destruction.
options.note: The angel explains identity and meaning, not a date.

options.text: The names of every future world leader.
options.note: The explanation concerns the symbolic meaning of the vision, not a list of names.

options.text: Nothing; the angel refuses to explain anything further.
options.note: The angel promises, and gives, a detailed explanation in the verses that follow.

quiz.q: According to the angel, what has God put into the hearts of the beast and the ten horns in verse 17?

options.text: To carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until God's words are fulfilled.
options.note: Revelation 17:17 gives this exact statement of God's sovereignty over evil's plans.

options.text: To repent and worship the Lamb.
options.note: The verse describes their unwitting service to God's purpose in judgment, not their repentance.

options.text: To rebuild the woman's kingdom stronger than before.
options.note: They destroy, rather than rebuild, the woman's kingdom.

options.text: Nothing; their actions happen entirely outside God's purposes.
options.note: The verse states plainly that God put this purpose into their hearts.

questions: Babylon is described as dazzling and seductive, dressed in gold, purple, and jewels, yet drunk on the blood of the saints. Where in your life is something seductive dressed up in a way that hides its true cost?

The very powers that carried the prostitute turn and destroy her. Have you seen alliances built on shared sin eventually turn on each other? What does that teach you about trusting anything built apart from God?
The Lamb triumphs, not by superior force in a fair fight, but simply because He is Lord of lords. Where do you need to rest in the certainty of His victory rather than your own strength?
God's called, chosen, and faithful ones share in the Lamb's triumph. What would it look like this week to actively identify yourself with Him rather than with the world's seductions?

The angel insists on explaining the mystery plainly rather than leaving John confused. When Scripture's symbols feel strange or frightening, how does it help to remember that God intends for His people to understand, not just to be unsettled?

translationNotes.note: Prostitute translates porne, sometimes rendered harlot in older translations; both render the same Greek word, and the choice reflects register rather than a difference in meaning.

Some manuscripts and translations print the name as a formal title in capitals, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, treating mystery as the first word of the inscription itself rather than a description of the name; the BSB's a mysterious name was written reflects one legitimate way to render the construction.

Was, and now is no more, but is about to come echoes and inverts the divine title who is, and who was, and who is to come from Revelation 1:4 and 1:8, a deliberate parody marking the beast as a false, blasphemous copy of God's eternity.

Seven mountains and the count of five fallen, one is, one not yet come are among Revelation's most debated numerical details; interpreters differ on whether to press them as a precise historical sequence or read them as symbolic of complete, worldly power.
